summary: BIER is a multicast forwarding architecture that needs no explicit tree-building protocol and keeps no per-tree state in transit routers. This RFC defines BGP extensions to carry the BIER-specific information that routers need to share, using BGP when it is the routing protocol in use.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of drawing a delivery map for each group, packets list who must get a copy. This lets routers share the info they need for that using BGP.

questions: how to advertise bier info in bgp

how does bgp signal bier information
what is a bier nexthop sub-tlv
subtitle: How BGP carries the per-router information that BIER multicast forwarding needs, without per-tree state.

tldr.problem: BIER forwards multicast without per-tree state in transit routers, but each BIER router still has to learn a small amount of per-router information such as its BFR-ID, supported BitStringLengths and label ranges.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional transitive BGP path attribute, the BIER attribute (type code 41), is attached to a router's host-address route and carries TLVs and sub-TLVs with that information. Receivers use it, plus a BIER Nexthop sub-TLV, to build their Bit Index Forwarding Tables.
tldr.outcome: BIER domains can use BGP as the signaling protocol, inside a single administrative domain. By default the attribute must not be sent to EBGP peers, so independent BIER domains are not joined by accident.

today: RFC 9793 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines BGP signaling for BIER inside a single administrative domain, building on the BIER architecture in RFC 8279.

sections.title: BIER Signaling Over BGP
sections.content:
Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER, RFC 8279) is a multicast forwarding architecture that needs no explicit tree-building protocol and keeps no per-tree multicast state in intermediate routers. Some information still has to be advertised, calculated and maintained, but it grows with the number of BIER routers, not with the number of trees.

RFC 9793 defines a new optional transitive BGP attribute, the BIER attribute, to convey that information, for example the Bit-Forwarding Router Identifier (BFR-ID) and the BitStringLength (BSL). It also defines how routers calculate BIER state from the advertisements. The signaling is meant for a single Administrative Domain.
sections.plainLanguage: BIER lets routers send a packet to many receivers without drawing a map for each group. This document teaches routers to share the few facts they need by using BGP, the messenger they already use.

sections.title: The BIER Path Attribute and TLVs
sections.content:
The BIER attribute is an optional, transitive BGP path attribute with type code 41 and variable length. It can be attached by the originator of a BGP UPDATE for NLRIs of AFI 1 or 2 and SAFI 1, 2 or 4, and it describes the BFR identified by the /32 (IPv4) or /128 (IPv6) host address prefix in the NLRI. When the attribute is present, that NLRI is called a BFR-prefix. Other AFIs and SAFIs, and non-host prefixes, are not defined here.

The attribute value is a series of TLVs, each with a 2-octet Type and a 2-octet Length, and no padding to 4-octet alignment. Unknown types MUST be preserved and propagated, and unknown TLVs MUST NOT make the NLRI or attribute malformed.

A BFR MUST include one BIER TLV (Type 1) for every sub-domain its prefix belongs to. Each holds a 1-octet Sub-domain, a 2-octet BFR-ID, a Reserved octet (SHOULD be 0 on transmission, MUST be ignored on reception) and sub-TLVs. If two BIER TLVs carry the same Sub-domain value, the entire BIER attribute MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The BIER attribute is a label stuck on a route. It says which BIER groups a router is in, what its seat number is, and how to reach it.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Nexthop Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Inside a BIER TLV, two encapsulation sub-TLVs tell receivers what to put on the wire. The MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV (Type 2) carries a Max SI, a 4-bit BS Len and a 20-bit Label. The labels from Label to Label + Max SI form a label range, one label per Set Identifier (SI), with the first label for SI=0. The non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV (Type 3) is the same shape but carries a 20-bit BIFT-id and defines a BIFT-id range.

Several rules protect against bad data. If the label for the Max SI exceeds the 20-bit range, that sub-TLV MUST be ignored. A repeated BitString length in MPLS sub-TLVs makes all of them in the BIER TLV ignored, and overlapping label ranges from the same BFR make all of that BFR's MPLS sub-TLVs ignored. For non-MPLS, a repeated BitString length makes the whole BIER TLV ignored. BIFT-id ranges may overlap label ranges, because they are different encapsulation types.

The BIER Nexthop sub-TLV (Type 4) holds a 4-octet IPv4 or 16-octet IPv6 address. It MAY be included, but at most once in each encapsulation sub-TLV or in the top-level BIER TLV, and it is used when computing BIFT entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router also says which numbered tickets it uses for each size of passenger list, and, if it wants, which neighbor should receive the packets for it.

sections.title: Originating and Re-advertising the Attribute
sections.content:
A Bit-Forwarding Egress Router (BFER) MUST attach a BIER attribute to its own host BFR-prefix, with one BIER TLV per supported sub-domain. Each BIER TLV MUST include an MPLS and/or non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV and MAY include a Nexthop sub-TLV. Without a Nexthop sub-TLV, receivers use the BIER prefix itself as the next hop.

A receiver first checks syntax: the BIER TLV lengths (with Type and Length fields) MUST add up to the attribute length, and sub-TLV lengths MUST add up to the TLV length. A failure makes the attribute malformed and the "attribute discard" action from RFC 7606 MUST be taken. Semantic failures only cause the offending TLVs to be ignored.

When a BFR re-advertises such a route, it SHOULD set the Nexthop sub-TLV to its own BIER prefix and then MUST replace the encapsulation sub-TLV with its own. If it does not update the Nexthop, it MUST NOT update the encapsulation sub-TLV, and it MUST NOT touch a BIER TLV for a sub-domain it does not support. For BitStringLengths it does not support, the original next hop is preserved inside the encapsulation sub-TLV. A non-BFR BGP speaker may still pass the attribute along, unchanged, because it is transitive.

Two different BFR-prefixes MUST NOT have the same non-zero BFR-ID in one sub-domain. If a receiver sees that, it MUST NOT use those prefixes for BIFT calculation in that sub-domain and SHOULD log an error.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router passes the message on, it may put its own name on it as the next stop. If it does not, it must leave the old details alone, like a mail sorter who does not rewrite someone else's address.

sections.title: Calculating the BIFT
sections.content:
As RFC 8279 notes, a Bit Index Forwarding Table (BIFT) is derived from the unicast FIB by adding BIER-specific information. For each sub-domain, a BFR goes through the BIER prefixes whose attribute has a BIER TLV for that sub-domain. For each non-zero BFR-ID it creates or updates a BIFT entry.

The entry's BFR neighbor is the Nexthop in the encapsulation sub-TLV if there is one, otherwise the Nexthop in the top-level BIER TLV, otherwise the BIER prefix itself. The BIER label or BIFT-id comes from the label range or BIFT-id range.

BIER traffic goes to that neighbor directly (the BIER header follows a Layer 2 header) when it is directly connected, or via a tunnel otherwise. How the tunnel is set up is out of scope; it can be any kind, such as an MPLS LSP or IP/GRE, as long as the tunnel header can indicate that the payload is BIER.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router builds a table that says, for every seat number, who to hand the packet to next. The details it learned from BGP fill in that table.

sections.title: A Worked Nexthop Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example has BFR1 connected through a non-BFR router to BFR2, which connects to BFER1, BFER2 and BFER3. Each BFER advertises its loopback with one BIER TLV per sub-domain, a non-zero BFR-ID and an MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV. BFER1 omits the Nexthop sub-TLV, while BFER2 and BFER3 include theirs.

When BFR2 re-advertises the routes toward the non-BFR, it adds a Nexthop sub-TLV to BFER1's route, updates the ones from BFER2 and BFER3, all with its own address, and replaces the MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV with its own labels. The non-BFR does nothing BIER-specific and passes the routes to BFR1 unchanged. BFR1 then uses BFR2's address from the Nexthop sub-TLV as the next hop. Because BFR2 is not directly connected, a tunnel must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A middle router that cannot read BIER just passes the note along. The routers at the ends can still see who to send to, and they use a tunnel to jump over the middle one.

sections.title: Keeping the Attribute Inside the Domain
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the BIER domain lines up with one Administrative Domain, which may contain several Autonomous Systems. BFR-prefixes are typically loopback addresses, spread through the domain but not needed outside it, much like Provider Edge loopbacks.

If prefixes with the BIER attribute leaked to a neighboring AD that also runs BIER, two domains that should be independent could be joined together, most likely with conflicting configurations, causing security risks and operational trouble. To prevent this, a boundary router that supports the attribute MUST support a per-EBGP-session or group policy saying whether the attribute is allowed, and by default it is not allowed. If not allowed, the attribute MUST NOT be sent to EBGP peers, and one received from such a peer MUST be treated as an unrecognized non-transitive attribute: quietly ignored and not passed on.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes are for your own club only. The doorkeeper does not pass them to other clubs unless told to.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The Security Considerations say that the document introduces no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 4271, RFC 8279 and its own operational considerations. In practice, the boundary policy above is the main protection.

IANA assigned path attribute code 41 to BIER and created the "BGP BIER TLV and Sub-TLV Types" registry. Its type field is 2 octets, value 0 is reserved, and new values are First Come First Served. Five initial values are allocated: 0 Reserved, 1 BIER TLV, 2 MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV, 3 non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV and 4 BIER Nexthop sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: There are no new dangers, and the main rule is to keep the notes inside your own club. The numbers for each kind of note were written in an official list.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value part in octets; 4 or other depending on sub-TLVs.

fields.name: Max SI
fields.desc: Maximum Set Identifier used for this sub-domain and BitString length.

fields.name: Label
fields.desc: First label in the label range.
